Vascular plants (from Latin vasculum 'duct'), also called tracheophytes ( UK : / ˈ t r æ k iː ə ˌ f aɪ t s / , [ 3 ] US : / ˈ t r eɪ k iː ə ˌ f aɪ t s / ) [ 4 ] or collectively Tracheophyta ( / ˌ t r eɪ k iː ˈ ɒ f ɪ t ə / ; [ 5 ] [ 6 ] [ 7 ] from Ancient Greek τραχεῖα ἀρτηρία ( trakheîa artēría ) ' windpipe ' and φυτά ( phutá ) ' plants ' ), [ 7 ] are plants that have lignified tissues (the xylem ) for conducting water and minerals throughout the plant. They also have a specialized non-lignified tissue (the phloem ) to conduct products of photosynthesis . The group includes most land plants ( c. 300,000 accepted known species) [ 8 ] excluding mosses .
